summary: Grays Harbor Co., WA lookout on the Clemons Tree Farm, built about 1940 and now gone; two footings found on a 2016 visit; private land under a permit.

facts.status_note: Sources say the lookout is gone. A 2016 visit found two footings nearly 20 feet apart; the author believes the tower was removed, not burned in place. A 2022 update on the same page says the summit was logged and four footings were placed about 20 feet downhill.
facts.agency: Clemons Tree Farm, owned by Weyerhaeuser Timber Company

access.note: Private tree-farm land. WillhiteWeb lists it under a Weyerhaeuser general access permit, with separate distances for vehicle and non-motorized permit holders. FFLOS lists the land as private.

events.note: WillhiteWeb: likely built in 1940 or within a few years prior. FFLOS: built in the 1940s.
WillhiteWeb visit: two footings found; author believes the lookout was removed and not burned in place
WillhiteWeb 2022 update: summit logged (clearcut); four footings placed about 20 feet downhill off the east side of the summit
Registered February 11, 2020 as US 1915, WA 446; nominated by Tammy McLeod

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FFLOS says built in the 1940s; WillhiteWeb says likely 1940 or a few years earlier. The story uses WillhiteWeb's estimate and keeps the decade wording from FFLOS out of the lead.

FFLOS and firelookout.com spell the farm Clemans; the WillhiteWeb body and HistoryLink spell it Clemons. HistoryLink gives both Charles H. and Charles L. Clemons. The story uses Clemons and leaves out the initial.
WillhiteWeb gives June 12, 1941 for the dedication; HistoryLink gives June 21, 1941. The story gives only the year, 1941.

corrections.proposed: Clemons Tree Farm, owned by Weyerhaeuser Timber Company
corrections.why: WillhiteWeb and HistoryLink both spell the farm's name Clemons, after logger Charles Clemons. The brief copied the FFLOS spelling.

sources.title: LEM Lookout Site - Clemans Tree Farm
Weyerhaeuser dedicates the nation's first tree farm near Montesano on June 21, 1941

notes_for_editor: The site is gone, with footings seen in a 2016 visit and a 2022 update that describes the summit as logged and four footings placed downhill. Access is permit-only on private land, so the story gives no route. The FFLOS page credits Eric Willhite for its site photo, but no image URL was read, so no photo is added. Staffing and fires are not in the sources, so they are omitted.
